BREAKING: Trade talks between the US and Canada have collapsed and the US has imposed new 50% tariffs on billions of dollars of Canadian goods.

Details include:

1. Canada's Prime Minister Carney vows to retaliate with "dollar for dollar" tariffs on the US

2. The tariffs will cover hundreds of items the US buys from Canada, such as plywood, liquor, electrical equipment and hockey gear, totaling ~$20 billion

3. US Trade Representative Greer said Canadian negotiators had "upset the balance" worked out over days of negotiations

4. The two sides had been discussing a deal that included lowering tariffs on Canadian steel and aluminum to 25% and autos to 15%

The US-Canada trade war appears to be back.

China’s industrial production rose +4.5% YoY in July, but posted its first monthly slowdown in 3 months.

At the same time, retail sales grew just +0.6% YoY, the 3rd-lowest reading in at least 18 months.

This comes as passenger vehicle purchases, the largest component of retail sales, dropped -21.0% YoY.

Over the same period, real estate investment collapsed -19.2% YoY, the largest drop on record.

China's economic slowdown is deepening across every major sector.

This also marks the 14th consecutive month of bullish positioning.

Furthermore, 37% of respondents expect double-digit earnings growth globally over the next 12 months, the highest percentage since August 2021.

Bullish sentiment is incredibly strong worldwide.

Martin Casado says capital used to be a lottery ticket, and AI made it a vending machine:

"If I'm training a model and I want it to be good at X, I can create an RL environment of X, or I can go pay someone to answer questions for X, and I can turn capital into being good at that X."

"The problem is you don't know what gets worse... Let's say you put in $10 to do this. I don't know if you get $9 back on the other side of that."

"What we've never been able to do in the history of this industry is put in $10 and get anything back."

"It was literally put in $10, engineer, engineer, engineer, wait two years, probably screw stuff up, it'll probably fail. But maybe on the other side you'll have a product you can monetize."

"Now it really is $10 in and then some amount out, pretty directly."

@martin_casado w/ @sophiadew and @theojaffee on MTS

China's property prices have now declined continuously since mid-2023.

It's 2008 for China's housing market.

The extra spread investors demand to hold EM credit over US credit has compressed to the narrowest on record, down from 60 basis points in the 2020 panic to about 15 today.

The compensation shrank. The risk did not. When you are paid the least in history to take EM credit risk, you hold the thinnest cushion right before you need one. The next global shock reprices EM dollar bonds with no spread buffer to absorb it. $EMB

For 20 years Japan was the cheapest place on earth to borrow. That just ended.

Japan's 10-year yield now sits a full point above China's, after trading 2 to 4 points below it for two decades.

Japan anchored the global carry trade because its bonds paid nothing. Now they pay, and Japanese money that funded the world comes home. Japan is the largest foreign holder of US Treasuries, so that repatriation pulls a bid out of the Treasury market and pushes US yields higher.

The bond vigilantes are back, and they picked France. French 10-year debt now yields 0.8% more than German bunds, the widest gap since the 2012 eurozone crisis.

This is about credit quality. A hung French parliament cannot pass a budget, so investors demand more to fund a government they no longer trust on its deficit.

France is the euro area's second-largest economy. A core sovereign spread blowing out is how a budget fight becomes an ECB problem, and the next leg lower in the euro.

A wall of cheap goods means every manufacturer that competes with China fights on price. That is exported deflation, and it lands on the industrial names in your portfolio.

I'd say it's already gained lots of traction! Lots of stocks down 50%.

My read is that this may seem like a compelling narrative, but there are so many exaggerations and logical leaps strung together to get there, that I find the conclusion pretty unlikely.

Take the claim that 35–40% of hyperscaler capex is going to memory. Bottom-up, I get closer to 20–25% (SemiAnalysis estimates 30%). And even that is a snapshot of a brutal shortage after the memory makers spent the 2022–24 downturn slashing production and capex.

Micro and Hynix are currently earning ~80% operating margins. I would not treat their one (admittedly huge) component of the AI stack as a permanently scarce input. New supply is being funded via SLAs, and not at these economics. Also, industry DRAM and NAND bit supply is already growing ~20% this year, quite contrary to his claim that memory makers are simply shipping "the same amount at higher prices." These little mistatements add up. I think he uses them to make overly provocative conclusions.

There are similar problems throughout. Like his fact that 60% of announced 2027 projects haven't broken ground. Mostly tells me some projects are late, not that capex "is NOT creating more data centers." 10 GW of new U.S. capacity finished through 1H26 says otherwise.

(I also don't necessarily agree that moving workloads from expensive frontier models to cheaper ones is demand destruction. Lowering the cost per task could just as easily increase total AI usage.)

You can follow the breadcrumbs from there.

For me, full disclosure, rather than try to time an exit and re-entry from these levels, unless something changes in the fundamentals, I'll probably just keep consolidating into my favorite names and buying them lower. Thats what the diversification was there for.
